title: Maximum Weight Independent Set on a Tree
directAnswer: Pick a subset of tree nodes with the largest total weight such that no two chosen nodes share an edge. The 'choose or skip' decision at each node depends only on its children, so a post-order DFS with two states per node solves it: dp[node][1] = best when you take node (children must be skipped), dp[node][0] = best when you skip node (each child takes its better option). The answer is max(dp[root][0], dp[root][1]). O(n) time.

remember.pattern: Post-order tree DP with two states per node: taken vs not taken
remember.formula:
dfs(node, parent):
    take = weight[node]
    skip = 0
    for child != parent:
        dfs(child, node)
        take += dp[child][0]            # child must be skipped
        skip += max(dp[child][0], dp[child][1])  # child free to choose
    dp[node][1] = take
    dp[node][0] = skip
rules: Two states per node: **taken** forces every child to the skipped state; **skipped** lets each child take its own max.
Combine children **independently** — subtrees do not interact except through the parent's choice.
Use **post-order**: a node's dp needs both children's dp values first.
The answer is **max(dp[root][0], dp[root][1])**, not just dp[root][1].
On a general (unrooted) tree, root it anywhere and pass the parent to avoid walking back up an edge.
whenToUse: Optimize over subsets of tree nodes with an adjacency (no-two-adjacent) constraint
House-Robber-style problems generalized from a line to a tree
Any 'select/skip with a local conflict' optimization on a tree
Counting or weighting where each node's choice only constrains its neighbors
antiSignals: Graph has cycles (not a tree) → maximum independent set is NP-hard in general; tree DP relies on no cycles
Constraint spans non-adjacent nodes (e.g. distance ≤ 2) → states must encode more than taken/skipped
You need the actual set, not just its weight → store back-pointers / reconstruct after the DP
The line case (array, not tree) → 1-D House Robber DP is simpler
remember.takeaway: Tree DP is 'solve each subtree, combine at the parent'. Encoding the parent's choice as a small state (here, taken or skipped) makes the children independent, so one post-order pass with O(1) work per node gives an O(n) optimum to a problem that is NP-hard on general graphs.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can define per-node states that capture the adjacency constraint (taken forces children skipped) and combine subtree results in a single post-order pass — recognizing this is House Robber lifted onto a tree.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using only one state per node (losing the information of whether the node was taken), returning dp[root][1] instead of the max of both states, or recursing without a parent guard and looping over the edge back to the parent.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it as House Robber III generalized, state the two recurrences crisply, justify post-order, and note that maximum independent set is NP-hard on general graphs but linear on trees because of the no-cycle structure.

problemStatement:
You are given a tree with `n` nodes, where node `i` has weight `w[i]`. Choose a subset `S` of nodes maximizing the total weight `Σ w[i]` over `i ∈ S`, subject to the constraint that ***no two chosen nodes are adjacent*** (connected by an edge).

Return the maximum achievable total weight.
constraints: Weights w[i] can be any integer (including negatives — skipping a negative node is allowed)
The graph is a tree: n − 1 edges, connected, no cycles
Total weight fits in 64-bit (use long in Java)
understanding: We want the heaviest set of nodes with no two touching. The crucial structural fact: once we decide whether a node is in the set, its children's options are constrained only by that one decision — taking the node bans its children, skipping it frees them. Subtrees are otherwise independent, so we can solve each subtree and merge the results at the parent. That independence is exactly what makes the tree version polynomial while the general-graph version is NP-hard.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it definitely a tree (no cycles)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. On a tree this is O(n) DP; on a general graph maximum independent set is NP-hard, so the tree structure is essential.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can weights be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The 'skip' option contributes 0 for an empty choice, so a node with negative weight is simply never taken — the max handles it automatically.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need the actual chosen nodes or just the total weight?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the weight here. To recover the set, store which branch won at each state and walk back down after the DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the tree rooted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If unrooted, root it at any node and pass the parent into the DFS so we never traverse back up the edge we came from.

examples.explanation: Take nodes 0(3), 3(1), and 4(6) = 10. Node 1 (weight 4) is adjacent to 0, 3, and 4, so taking it would block all three; skipping it to take the lighter trio wins. The set {0,3,4} is independent: 0 only touches 1 and 2, both skipped.
One node, no edges — take it.
Take the two ends (4 + 4 = 8) rather than the heavier-looking middle (5). The classic House Robber trade-off on a line.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Enumerate Every Independent Subset
approaches.whenToMention: Frame the problem with this, then show how local decisions collapse the exponential search into O(n).
hints: Every node is either in the set or out. Try all 2^n assignments and keep the heaviest that is independent.
Check independence by verifying no edge has both endpoints chosen, then sum the weights.
Exponential — but it reveals the real structure: a node's validity depends only on its neighbors, so the decisions are local.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are 2^n subsets; validating and summing each is O(n), giving O(n·2^n). Hopeless beyond ~25 nodes, but it defines what 'optimal' means.
approaches.explanation:
The definitional approach is to try every subset.

**Enumerate.** Each node is independently in or out, so there are `2^n` candidate subsets. For each, confirm no edge connects two chosen nodes and total the weights; keep the best valid total.

**Why it is correct but useless at scale.** It literally searches the entire solution space, so it cannot miss the optimum — but `2^n` explodes past a couple dozen nodes.

**The observation that rescues it.** Validity is *local*: a chosen node only forbids its direct neighbors. On a tree, a node's only neighbors are its parent and children, and the subtrees hanging off different children share no edges. So the choice inside one child's subtree does not constrain another child's subtree — they interact solely through whether the parent is taken. That independence means we can solve each subtree once and combine, replacing the exponential enumeration with a single pass.
approaches.insight: The leap from exponential to linear is the realization that the no-adjacency constraint is purely local on a tree: fixing one node's in/out status fully decouples its children's subtrees. Capture that one bit of context as a DP state and the search collapses.

java.explanation: Every subset of nodes as a bitmask — 2^n of them.
Reject any subset that includes both ends of an edge.

python.line: if any((mask >> u) & 1 and (mask >> v) & 1 for u, v in edges):
python.explanation: Skip masks where some edge is fully chosen — not independent.

python.line: total = sum(w[i] for i in range(n) if (mask >> i) & 1)
python.explanation: Sum the weights of the chosen nodes.

pitfalls: Treating it as feasible for large n — 2^n is exponential.
Forgetting the empty set (weight 0) as a valid baseline for all-negative weights.
Re-checking the same subtree decisions across masks — the redundancy the DP removes.

approaches.name: Tree DP — Two States per Node (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. 'Post-order DFS; each node returns the best taking it and the best skipping it.'
hints: Define two values per node: dp[node][1] = best total in node's subtree WHEN node is taken; dp[node][0] = best WHEN node is skipped.
If you take the node, no child may be taken, so add each child's dp[child][0]. If you skip the node, each child is free, so add max(dp[child][0], dp[child][1]).
Post-order: compute both children's states first, then the parent's. The answer is max(dp[root][0], dp[root][1]).
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single post-order DFS visits each node once and does O(deg) work combining its children; summed over the tree that is O(n) total (each edge handled once). The recursion stack and dp arrays are O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Encode the only thing a child needs to know about its parent's decision as a per-node state, and the subtrees decouple.

**The two states.** For each node define:
- `dp[node][1]` — the maximum total weight in `node`'s subtree *given that `node` is taken*.
- `dp[node][0]` — the maximum total weight in `node`'s subtree *given that `node` is skipped*.

**The recurrences.** Process children first (post-order), then combine:
- If `node` is **taken**, none of its children may be taken (they are adjacent to it). So `dp[node][1] = w[node] + Σ dp[child][0]` over all children.
- If `node` is **skipped**, each child may independently do whatever is best for it. So `dp[node][0] = Σ max(dp[child][0], dp[child][1])`.

**Why the children are independent.** Two children of the same node live in disjoint subtrees joined only through that node. Once the parent's taken/skipped status is fixed, no constraint links one child's subtree to another's, so we can optimize each child separately and add the results. This is precisely why a single bit of state per node is enough.

**Why post-order.** Each recurrence reads the children's dp values, so every child must be finished before its parent — left/right (or all children) first, then the node.

**The answer.** At the root there is no parent to constrain it, so either state is allowed: `max(dp[root][0], dp[root][1])`. Returning only `dp[root][1]` wrongly forces the root into the set.

**Negative weights for free.** Because `dp[node][0]` sums `max(skip, take)` and a taken negative node would only lower the total, the max naturally declines to take nodes that hurt — no special case needed.

**This is House Robber on a tree.** House Robber III is exactly this with weights on a binary tree; the line version (plain House Robber) is the same recurrence on a path. Recognizing the family is the fastest way to the right code.
approaches.insight: The whole trick is choosing a state that makes subtrees independent. 'Taken vs skipped' is the minimal context a parent must hand down, because adjacency only reaches one level. Once decisions decouple, an NP-hard general-graph problem becomes a linear post-order scan — a recurring lesson in tree DP.

dryRun.intro: dp[node] = (skip, take). Leaves first, then up. Children must skip if parent is taken.

code.python:
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

class TreeMIS:
    def max_weight(self, n: int, root: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int]], w: list[int]) -> int:
        adj = defaultdict(list)
        for u, v in edges:
            adj[u].append(v)
            adj[v].append(u)
        dp = [[0, 0] for _ in range(n)]   # dp[node][0]=skip, dp[node][1]=take
        parent = [root] * n
        order = []
        seen = [False] * n
        stack = [root]
        seen[root] = True
        while stack:                       # iterative traversal, chain-safe
            node = stack.pop()
            order.append(node)
            for nxt in adj[node]:
                if not seen[nxt]:
                    seen[nxt] = True
                    parent[nxt] = node
                    stack.append(nxt)
        # Children before parents: reverse the discovery order.
        for node in reversed(order):
            take = w[node]
            skip = 0
            for child in adj[node]:
                if child == parent[node]:
                    continue
                take += dp[child][0]
                skip += max(dp[child][0], dp[child][1])
            dp[node][1] = take
            dp[node][0] = skip
        return max(dp[root][0], dp[root][1])

java.explanation: Two states per node: index 0 = skip this node, index 1 = take it.
Reverse discovery order processes children before parents — an iterative post-order.
Skip the edge back to the parent so we only recurse into real children.
Taking node forbids each child → add the child's skip value.
Skipping node frees each child → add the child's better option.
Root has no parent, so either state is allowed — take the max.

Either take the center (skip all leaves) or skip the center (take every positive leaf); the DP compares both.

pitfalls: Using one state per node — you lose whether the node was taken, breaking the parent's recurrence.
Returning dp[root][1] instead of max(dp[root][0], dp[root][1]).
Recursing without a parent check — infinite loop over the parent edge on an undirected adjacency list.
Deep recursion on a chain of 10⁵ nodes — use an iterative post-order to avoid stack overflow.

commonMistakes: Tracking only one value per node instead of separate taken/skipped states.
Returning the 'root taken' value rather than the max over both root states.
Looping back over the parent edge because the DFS has no parent guard.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: One state per node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A child needs to know its own best total in BOTH cases — when the parent is taken (child forced to skip) and when the parent is skipped (child free). Collapsing to a single value loses the case the parent needs.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def dfs(node, parent):
    best = w[node]
    for c in children: best += dfs(c, node)   # single value, no skip case
    return best
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
def dfs(node, parent):
    take, skip = w[node], 0
    for c in children:
        ct, cs = dfs(c, node)            # (take, skip) for the child
        take += cs
        skip += max(ct, cs)
    return take, skip

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning only the taken state
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The root has no parent constraining it, so skipping the root can be better (e.g. a heavy node deep in the tree). Return the max of both root states.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return dp[root][1];                 // forces the root into the set

commonMistakesDetailed.title: No parent guard on an undirected tree
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adjacency lists store each edge in both directions. Without skipping the parent, the DFS revisits the parent as a 'child' and recurses forever.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for child in adj[node]:
    dfs(child, node)               # also recurses into the parent
